clue.text: Argentine sea cook

blocks.note: first meaning: argentine is an old adjective for silvery, from Latin argentum
second meaning: Long John, the ship's cook in Treasure Island, by surname

explanation.surface: A chef working aboard ship who hails from Argentina.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Argentine' looks like the nationality, but it is the adjective meaning silvery; the sea cook is Long John Silver of Treasure Island.
explanation.definitionFit: Argentine describes the colour of the precious metal, and the pirate cook's surname in Stevenson's novel is the same word.

clue.text: School's head let one out for interval

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: the initial of school
to let one out is to emit one, giving off a single thing

explanation.surface: The headteacher released a pupil early for break time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interval' here is musical, not a school break or playtime.
explanation.definitionFit: In music this is the smallest step in Western scales, half a whole tone, so it is an interval between pitches.

clue.text: Weapon extended with respectful salutation

blocks.note: long means stretched out or extended
a bow is a polite bend of the body in greeting

explanation.surface: An arm is held out while giving a courteous greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: The tall English bow used at Agincourt is a classic medieval projectile weapon drawn by archers.

clue.text: Choose examination for this sort of college

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective; the clue defines it by the noun phrase it qualifies

blocks.note: to elect is to choose by vote
an oral is a spoken exam

explanation.surface: Pick an entrance test for a certain kind of college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'College' suggests a university; it is the body that formally picks the US president.
explanation.definitionFit: The American body of delegates that formally chooses the president is known by this adjective plus the word college.

clue.text: Policeman takes note to part of Yard

blocks.note: a flat is a note lowered by a semitone
a yard is made up of three feet

explanation.surface: A detective collects a written message and takes it to Scotland Yard.
explanation.definitionFit: Flatfoot is American slang for a beat cop, from the plodding gait of officers who walk all day.

clue.text: Police, damn it, involved with my business

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the letters are mixed into a fresh order

blocks.note: fodder, taken as written
fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone cursing that the police have got mixed up in their firm.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm whose owners' liability is capped at their investment is a common legal form of commercial enterprise.

clue.text: Keep a horse on canal, say

blocks.note: first meaning: the fortified stronghold of a castle
second meaning: one that pulls a boat by rope, as a barge horse did along the towpath

explanation.surface: An instruction to stable a horse beside the canal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' looks like a verb about stabling, but it is the noun for a castle stronghold.
explanation.definitionFit: A keep is a castle's main fortified building, and a barge horse is literally one who tows.

clue.text: Love-song to write inside or outdoors

indicators.note: inside places one word within the pair either side of it

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O
to pen is to write
an air is a tune or song

explanation.surface: Pen a love song indoors or out in the fresh air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love-song' is one hyphenated thing in the surface, but split it: love and song are separate pieces with write placed between.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase, often hyphenated as an adjective, describes events held outside rather than under a roof.

clue.text: Coin for examiner in queer street

blocks.note: first meaning: an old English silver coin, later slang for sixpence
second meaning: one who tries or checks something

explanation.surface: An inspector, short of money, needs a coin.
explanation.walkthrough: To be in Queer Street is British slang for being in debt; the phrase only dresses the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A tester was a Tudor shilling and later a sixpence, and anyone who tries something out is also one.

clue.text: Spy chief is right to steal

blocks.note: M is the head of the secret service in the James Bond stories
taken as written
appropriate means suitable or right

explanation.surface: An intelligence boss claims it is justified to take something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' looks like R; it is a whole synonym, suitable.
explanation.definitionFit: To take funds or goods dishonestly for one's own use is embezzlement, a form of theft.

clue.text: Art movement's idiosyncrasy

blocks.note: first meaning: the sixteenth-century Italian style after the High Renaissance
second meaning: a habitual quirk of speech or gesture

explanation.surface: An artistic school's peculiar quirk.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the elongated, artificial style of late Renaissance painting and any personal habit or affected peculiarity of behaviour.

clue.text: Birds run in all directions

indicators.note: in places the short word within the longer one that follows

blocks.note: the four compass points West, East, North, South
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Startled birds scatter every which way.
explanation.definitionFit: Wrens are tiny brown songbirds common in gardens, so the plural is a fair synonym for a group of birds.

clue.text: She needs a change of habitat

indicators.note: a change of something means its letters are altered into a fresh order

blocks.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman, or perhaps an animal, wants to move to new surroundings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' is the whole definition: the answer is a woman's first name, as in Beatrix Potter's Tabitha Twitchit.
explanation.definitionFit: A female given name stands for a woman, so the pronoun can define any girl's name in crossword convention.

clue.text: Row of houses in high-rise flat area

blocks.note: first meaning: a line of joined houses, typical of British streets
second meaning: a raised level platform, as on a hillside or beside a building

explanation.surface: A street of homes inside a tower block of flats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High-rise flat' suggests apartments in a tower block, but read it as a raised, level patch of ground.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both a continuous row of linked dwellings and a level raised platform of earth or paving.

clue.text: More modern vessel heading North? On the contrary

indicators.note: this reverses the stated arrangement, so the compass point comes first and leads the container

blocks.note: N is the compass abbreviation
a ewer is a large water jug

explanation.surface: A newer ship sets course northward, or perhaps not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel heading North' would put the jug first; 'on the contrary' makes North head the vessel instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A comparative adjective meaning more recent in origin, the plain opposite of older.

clue.text: Extreme form of treatment patient won't stand for?

definitions.text: Extreme form of treatment patient won't stand for?

blocks.note: surface reading: a drastic, harsh medical therapy
setter's reading: care of the extremities, the feet, during which the client must sit and cannot stand

explanation.surface: A drastic therapy that no patient would tolerate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extreme' points to the body's extremities, and 'won't stand for' is literal: you cannot stand while your feet are being treated.
explanation.definitionFit: This is cosmetic care of the feet and toenails, the body's lowest extremities, given while the client sits.

clue.text: Job wasn't made easier by one, however

definitions.text: Job wasn't made easier by one, however

blocks.note: surface reading: a piece of work that stayed hard
setter's reading: the biblical Job, whose friends came to console him but only added to his misery

explanation.surface: A task that some helper failed to lighten.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on 'Job' is hidden at the start of the clue: it is the Old Testament sufferer, and the phrase is a byword for a consoler who makes things worse.
explanation.definitionFit: A consoler is someone who soothes grief, and the Bible's Job had three notoriously unhelpful ones.

clue.text: Corresponding but never meeting

blocks.note: first meaning: matching or analogous
second meaning: of lines that stay the same distance apart forever

explanation.surface: Pen friends who write but never get together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corresponding' suggests exchanging letters, which fits the surface of friends who never meet.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means analogous or similar, and in geometry describes lines that run side by side without intersecting.

clue.text: Such a boring task can make you prosperous

blocks.note: surface reading: a tedious, dull chore
setter's reading: the job of drilling down for water, read as a phrase of three words

explanation.surface: Tedious work, it is suggested, is the way to get rich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' means drilling, not dull: a shaft to be sunk for water is a task to do, and the phrase together means rich.
explanation.definitionFit: The hyphenated idiom describes a comfortably wealthy family, a standard synonym for affluent or prosperous.

clue.text: Try to influence jury to hold tight

blocks.note: first meaning: a legal term, the offence of corrupting jurors being embracery
second meaning: hug or clasp in the arms

explanation.surface: Attempting to sway jurors so as to grip them firmly.
explanation.walkthrough: The legal sense is rare: embracery is the old crime of trying to corrupt or bribe a jury.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides hugging someone closely, the verb is an old legal word for illegally swaying jurors, hence embracery.

clue.text: Ancient lawmaker, a princess of Colchis

blocks.note: the laws of the Medes and Persians were proverbially unalterable
taken as written

explanation.surface: A list of figures from antiquity: a legislator and a Colchian royal.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition here includes its own 'a', so the wordplay supplies the article separately from the first phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the sorceress who helped Jason win the Golden Fleece was daughter of King Aeetes of Colchis.

clue.text: Plan unclear about Indian city

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the other

blocks.note: dim means faint or indistinct
the city of the Taj Mahal

explanation.surface: A vague scheme concerning a city in India.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawing or chart showing how parts are arranged is a schematic plan.

clue.text: Tries, for example, a large number

blocks.note: first meaning: points gained in a game, a rugby try being one kind
second meaning: lots

explanation.surface: An example of many attempts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tries' looks like attempts; it is the rugby touchdown, worth points, so an example of scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugby tries are examples of points tallied, and the plural of twenty also means a great many.

clue.text: Last employer's drink

blocks.note: first meaning: a shoemaker, who works on a last, the foot-shaped mould
second meaning: an iced drink of wine or sherry with sugar and fruit

explanation.surface: The final boss one worked for has a favourite tipple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last' looks like 'final', but it is the shoemaker's mould, so the last employer is one who uses a last.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoe mender uses the wooden last, and the same word names a sweet iced cocktail of wine and fruit.

clue.text: Losing his head. Mahler turned to another composer

indicators.note: losing a head means the opening letter is cut off
turned means the remaining letters are rearranged into new order

blocks.note: the Austrian composer, taken as written

explanation.surface: A composer, beheaded, is turned into a different composer.
explanation.walkthrough: Franz Lehar wrote the operetta The Merry Widow.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Lehar was a Hungarian composer of operettas, so he is a composer other than Mahler.

clue.text: How Romans kept things in proportion

blocks.note: surface reading: a question about ancient Roman tidiness or balance

blocks.clueFragment: How Romans kept things in proportion
blocks.note: setter's reading: the Latin phrase the Romans would use for proportionately

explanation.surface: A historical question about how the ancient Romans kept a sense of balance.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a Latin phrase still used in English, so it is literally how Romans would say it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin expression means according to rate, the standard way of saying shared out proportionally.

clue.text: Swimmers approaching middle section

indicators.note: the central part of the next word is lifted out, leaving its ends behind

blocks.note: the core letters, with the first two and last three removed

explanation.surface: Swimmers nearing the halfway mark of a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmers' suggests people in a pool; the fish name is the same in singular and plural.
explanation.definitionFit: These are freshwater fish of the carp family, and the plural is unchanged, so they are swimmers.

clue.text: Plainly cooked, without dressing

blocks.note: first meaning: a menu term for food served simply, without sauce
second meaning: naked, wearing no clothes

explanation.surface: Simple food served with no salad dressing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressing' looks like salad dressing, which fits the first half; it really means clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means in a natural state, used of plain cookery and, humorously, of a nude person.

clue.text: Pikestaff?

blocks.note: surface reading: the wooden shaft of a pike, as in 'plain as a pikestaff'
setter's reading: staff in the sense of personnel, soldiers armed with pikes

explanation.walkthrough: Split it as pike staff: a body of workers who carry pikes, soldiers with long thrusting weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers armed with long-shafted thrusting weapons were a fighting staff of pike or lance bearers.

clue.text: First mate holds the edge

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so one word surrounds the other

blocks.note: a pal is a friend
a rim is a border or edge

explanation.surface: A ship's first mate keeps the advantage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First mate' reads as a ship's officer, but 'First' is the definition and 'mate' a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Primal means original or earliest in time, as in primal instincts, so it equals first.
